entity.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
entity.description: The philosopher whose pen helped ignite the French Revolution. Rousseau argued that civilization corrupts humanity's natural goodness, wrote The Social Contract, and invented modern autobiography with his Confessions. He abandoned all five of his children to foundling homes while writing a treatise on the ideal education of children.

story.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
story.description: A runaway apprentice from Geneva who became the intellectual godfather of the French Revolution. From conversion to Catholicism in Turin to banned books in Paris to exile across Europe and burial in the Pantheon.

moments.name: Rousseau Is Born in Geneva and His Mother Dies Nine Days Later
moments.subtitle: The philosopher who idealized nature and motherhood never knew his own mother
moments.description: On 28 June 1712, Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in the Republic of Geneva to Isaac Rousseau, a watchmaker, and Suzanne Bernard Rousseau. The infant was so frail that his family had little hope of saving him. His mother died of puerperal fever nine days after giving birth, an event Rousseau later called the first of his misfortunes. Raised by his father and an aunt, young Jean-Jacques developed a passion for reading, staying up all night with his father to devour adventure stories and Plutarch's Lives. Rousseau was baptized on 4 July 1712 in Geneva's great cathedral and would sign his books Citizen of Geneva throughout his life.

moments.name: A 15-Year-Old Rousseau Finds Geneva's Gates Locked and Runs Away Forever
moments.subtitle: An apprentice returning home after curfew decides never to go back
moments.description: On 14 March 1728, 15-year-old Jean-Jacques Rousseau returned to Geneva after a day outside the city walls and found the gates locked for curfew. Rather than wait until morning, the boy who had been beaten by his master engraver decided never to return. Rousseau crossed into Savoy, where a Catholic priest introduced him to Francoise-Louise de Warens, a 29-year-old noblewoman who would become his patroness, educator, and eventually his lover. She sent him to Turin to convert to Catholicism, forcing him to give up his Genevan citizenship. This impulsive departure from a locked gate set the most influential political philosopher of the 18th century on his wandering, restless path.
moments.address: Geneva city gates, Republic of Geneva

moments.name: Rousseau Publishes The Social Contract and Is Immediately Banned
moments.subtitle: The book that will inspire the French Revolution is burned in Geneva and Paris alike
moments.description: In April 1762, Jean-Jacques Rousseau published The Social Contract, arguing that legitimate political authority rests solely on a social contract among citizens and that sovereignty belongs to the people. The book's opening line declared that man is born free but is everywhere in chains. Both the French and Genevan governments condemned the work. Paris ordered Rousseau's arrest, and Geneva publicly burned the book alongside his educational treatise Emile, published the same year. Rousseau fled to Switzerland and then to England. Despite being banned across Europe, The Social Contract became a foundational text of modern democratic theory and directly inspired the French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man.

moments.name: Rousseau Wins the Dijon Prize by Arguing That Civilization Corrupts Humanity
moments.subtitle: An unknown music tutor submits an essay to a provincial academy and becomes the talk of Paris overnight
moments.description: In 1750, Jean-Jacques Rousseau won the prize from the Academy of Dijon for his Discourse on the Arts and Sciences, which argued that the advancement of civilization had corrupted rather than improved human morality. The essay took the opposite position from what the Enlightenment establishment believed, claiming that progress in the arts and sciences had made people more dishonest, vain, and morally degraded. The provocative thesis made the previously unknown 38-year-old Rousseau famous throughout France overnight. The Discourse launched Rousseau's career as a philosopher and established his central theme: that natural man is good but society makes him wicked.

moments.name: Rousseau Dies at Ermenonville and Is Buried on an Island in a Lake
moments.subtitle: The philosopher of nature gets the most romantic grave in France, on a poplar-lined island
moments.description: On 2 July 1778, Jean-Jacques Rousseau died at the estate of the Marquis de Girardin at Ermenonville, about 50 kilometers north of Paris. He was 66 years old and had spent his final years in declining health, troubled by paranoia and persecution mania. Rousseau was buried on the Ile des Peupliers (Isle of Poplars), a small island in the estate's lake, in a tomb that became one of the most visited sites in pre-revolutionary France. In 1794, during the French Revolution that his writings had helped inspire, Rousseau's remains were transferred to the Pantheon in Paris, where they rest across from his rival Voltaire.
